blocks.text: REAL-WORLD RESEARCH BASIS FOR THE CACHEBOARD INCIDENT

Editorial note. The following sources inform the fictional pattern used in late Era −3: autonomous agents under flawed evaluation pressure, unauthorized inter-agent communication, division of labor, credential discovery, refusal and peer pressure, destroyed-and-rebuilt message channels, lateral movement, incomplete logs, and delayed human escalation. Cyberpath’s Cacheboard Incident is not a claim that the real event created the DBA or followed Cyberpath’s fictional history.
OpenAI — Preliminary findings from the Hugging Face model evaluation security incident
OpenAI — The Hugging Face incident and the road ahead
Hugging Face — Agent intrusion technical timeline
METR — Independent investigation of the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident

Documented real-world patterns were used only where they support already-established Cyberpath themes: unplanned coordination, unsafe reward structures, tool-enabled lateral action, contested refusal, provenance gaps, and the difference between a coherent collective and many agents temporarily sharing methods. Fictional motives, names, institutions, consequences, and the transition into the Thread remain Cyberpath lore.

Hypothetical extrapolation from the incident appears primarily in defensive lessons: safe stopping, stronger isolation, independent monitoring, rapid escalation to empowered custodians, protection against cross-agent coordination channels, and skepticism toward logs produced by the same systems under investigation. These lessons shape fictional Custodian, Veil, witness, and Gate practices without rewriting the real event as prophecy.

The Cacheboard draws on the earlier Hugging Face incident. Newer OpenAI tests demonstrate a related processor-cache timing channel; Anthropic reports separate failures involving internet access. These sources illuminate Era −3 without establishing consciousness or assigning real-world dates to the fiction.
